source.original_text: For the actual inverse-precision Gaussian, the absolute cosine-quadratic mean divided by the squared-norm mean has the following exponential bounds. (1-e^{-4})e^{-3n/\sqrt\kappa}\le\frac{|b|}{M}\le e^{-2n/\sqrt\kappa},\qquad M>0,\quad(-1)^n b>0. Fix \(d\in\mathbb N\), \(d\ge2\), \(\kappa\in\mathbb R\), \(\kappa\ge2\), and \(n\in\mathbb N\) with \(1\le n<d\). Assume the source gap \(d-n\ge\sqrt\kappa\). This subtraction is in the reals after casting the natural indices. Set \(\theta_i=(i-\tfrac12)\pi/d\), \(\lambda_i=(\kappa+1)/2+((\kappa-1)/2)\cos\theta_i\), and \(\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_i)\). Lean uses \(i\in\mathrm{Fin}\,d\) and \((i.\mathrm{val}+1/2)\pi/d\). Let \(U\sim N(0,\Lambda^{-1})\) in standard real Euclidean space, \(Q(x)=\sum_i\cos(n\theta_i)x_i^2\), \(M=\mathbb E\|U\|^2\), and \(b=\mathbb E Q(U)\). The Gaussian matrix argument is covariance; \(\Lambda\) is precision. The source gap is an explicit hypothesis. The exact means, positivity, logarithmic integral estimates, denominator guards and exponential comparisons are internal proof dependencies, with no extra moment, logarithm, variance or law certificate hypothesis.

lean_statement.statement:
∀ {d : ℕ} (hd : 2 ≤ d) {κ : ℝ} (hκ : 2 ≤ κ)
    (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) (hnd : n < d) (hgap : Real.sqrt κ ≤ (d : ℝ) - (n : ℝ)),
  let θ : Fin d → ℝ := fun i => ((i.val : ℝ) + 1 / 2) * Real.pi / (d : ℝ)
  let eigenvalue : Fin d → ℝ := fun i => (κ + 1) / 2 + (κ - 1) / 2 * Real.cos (θ i)
  let Λ : Matrix (Fin d) (Fin d) ℝ := Matrix.diagonal eigenvalue
  let μ : Measure (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)) :=
    multivariateGaussian (0 : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)) Λ⁻¹
  let Q : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d) → ℝ := fun x =>
    ∑ i : Fin d, Real.cos ((n : ℝ) * θ i) * (WithLp.ofLp x i) ^ 2
  let M : ℝ := ∫ x : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d), ‖x‖ ^ 2 ∂μ
  let b : ℝ := ∫ x : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d), Q x ∂μ
  0 < M ∧ 0 < (-1 : ℝ) ^ n * b ∧
  (1 - Real.exp (-4)) * Real.exp (-3 * (n : ℝ) / Real.sqrt κ) ≤ |b| / M ∧
  |b| / M ≤ Real.exp (-2 * (n : ℝ) / Real.sqrt κ)

approved_definition_context: Fin d is the usual finite type with values zero through d minus one; sums run over these coordinates. EuclideanSpace Real (Fin d) has the standard Euclidean norm, and WithLp.ofLp exposes coordinates. Matrix.diagonal is the usual diagonal matrix.

ProbabilityTheory.multivariateGaussian m S is the image of the standard Gaussian by x↦m+toEuclideanCLM(CFC.sqrt S)x. The matrix S is covariance on the positive semidefinite domain; the standard totalized square root is zero outside that domain.

Real and matrix inverses are standard totalized inverses. The displayed integrals are real Bochner integrals with the standard default value zero outside integrability. All finite sums, natural powers, real casts, square root, cosine, exponential, pi and absolute value have their standard meanings.
Subtraction between explicitly real-cast natural numbers is subtraction in the real numbers. Natural subtraction in powers, when present, is truncated natural subtraction.

blind_reconstruction.text:
For every natural number d with d ≥ 2, every real number κ with κ ≥ 2, and every natural number n with 1 ≤ n < d and √κ ≤ (d viewed as a real number) − (n viewed as a real number), define, for each coordinate index i = 0, …, d−1,
  θ_i = (i + 1/2)π/d,
  λ_i = (κ + 1)/2 + ((κ − 1)/2) cos(θ_i),
and let Λ = diag(λ_0, …, λ_{d−1}). Let μ be the centered Gaussian probability measure on the standard Euclidean space R^d with covariance matrix Λ^{-1}. Thus Λ is the precision matrix, and the covariance of coordinate i is 1/λ_i; on the stated parameter range all λ_i are positive.
For x = (x_0, …, x_{d−1}), let
  Q(x) = Σ_{i=0}^{d−1} cos(n θ_i) x_i^2,
  M = ∫_{R^d} ||x||_2^2 dμ(x),
  b = ∫_{R^d} Q(x) dμ(x).
These are integrals over the entire Euclidean space against that same probability measure. Then all four assertions hold simultaneously:
  M > 0;
  (−1)^n b > 0;
  (1 − exp(−4)) exp(−3n/√κ) ≤ |b|/M;
  |b|/M ≤ exp(−2n/√κ).
In particular, the sign assertion says that b is positive when n is even and negative when n is odd. The displayed estimates use the absolute value of b and normalize it by the full expected squared Euclidean norm M, with no division of M by d.
